tldr: Researchers have developed RIPPLE, a reinforcement learning framework that enables stable walking, balancing, and consecutive jumping on large-deformation elastic terrains like trampolines using only proprioception without external sensors, successfully achieving zero-shot transfer to a real humanoid robot.
hero_caption: Schematic of the proposed ElasticMembrane elastic ground model. A collision mesh, a pretensioned tendon lattice, and a fixed outer frame share point-mass nodes, efficiently simulating whole-surface deflection, energy storage, and rebound with delayed contact dynamics on the GPU.
overview:
Conventional bipedal robot control typically assumes non-deforming rigid floors or yielding terrains like sand where deformation is purely localized directly under the foot. However, the story changes completely on elastic terrains such as suspension bridges, safety nets, mattresses, or trampolines. Stepping down causes the entire surface to deflect significantly, and stored elastic energy keeps the surface oscillating even after contact breaks. Furthermore, load applied at one foot spatially propagates to the support point of the other foot, meaning the state of the terrain at the next touchdown strongly depends on the robot's own preceding actions.

To tackle this spatio-temporal coupling, the authors developed RIPPLE, a sim-to-real learning framework. At its core is ElasticMembrane, a model that reproduces the elastic dynamics of a thin membrane using a pretensioned mass-spring lattice. By integrating this into the GPU-parallel physics engines MuJoCo-Warp and MJLab, they established an environment capable of reinforcement learning while rapidly solving contact surface deflection and rebound.

Training begins from rigid-ground walking skills and applies a staged curriculum using solely proprioception—such as joint angles and angular velocities—without any cameras or foot force sensors as a shared interface. In real-world experiments using the MagicBot Z1 humanoid, the policy achieved zero-shot transfer without hardware recalibration, demonstrating resilience against human pushes on a trampoline, 15 consecutive jumps, and walking onto the trampoline from a rigid platform. This groundbreaking research proves that humanoids can master large-deformation, dynamic surfaces by literally 'riding the wave.'
contributions: Integrated ElasticMembrane, a pretensioned mass-spring mesh inspired by membrane mechanics, into MuJoCo-Warp/MJLab to build a GPU-parallel simulation environment modeling coupled elastic deformation and humanoid dynamics.

Proposed a staged policy transfer method adapting rigid-ground locomotion to elastic-terrain balancing and jumping, achieving zero-shot transfer to a physical humanoid using only proprioception without vision or foot force sensing.
Demonstrated for the first time on a real humanoid-trampoline setup stable balance against human pushes and bed shakes, over 15 consecutive jumps, and entry walking from a rigid platform.

Quantitatively demonstrated high zero-shot generalization across multiple simulated terrain models, stiffness variations (0.35x to 2.8x), bed sizes up to 7 m, and seven additional application scenarios such as suspension bridges and bamboo rafts.

sections.heading: Why walking on a trampoline is hard—and how this paper solves it
sections.summary: Deploying humanoids in real-world environments requires adapting to elastically deforming surfaces like suspension bridges and nets. However, reinforcement learning in dynamic environments where the entire surface deforms and rebounds continuously has remained unsolved. This paper introduces RIPPLE to address this challenge.
sections.details:
For humanoid robots to be deployed in disaster response, infrastructure inspection, or home assistance, they must navigate soft, deformable terrains such as suspension bridges, safety nets, floating platforms, and mattresses, rather than just rigid flat ground.

Past legged robotics research has studied yielding surfaces like sand or mud, where the ground deforms purely locally under the foot. In contrast, elastic terrains like trampolines exhibit fundamentally different behavior. Foot loads deflect the entire surface and store elastic energy, vibrations persist after liftoff, and loading one foot alters the support conditions beneath the other. In other words, a robot's past footfalls dictate its future footing dynamics.

While model predictive control has previously enabled quadrupeds to jump on trampolines, learning-based control deployed on physical humanoids to master this dynamic coupling remained unexplored.

This study presents RIPPLE (Robust Interaction via Proprioceptive Policies on Large-deformation Elastic terrain). RIPPLE implements the thin-membrane model ElasticMembrane on a GPU simulator and uses only proprioception (joint encoders and IMU readings) to transfer skills progressively from rigid ground to elastic terrain. Relying on no vision or tactile foot sensors, it achieves zero-shot balance, consecutive jumping, and rigid-to-elastic transition on a physical MagicBot Z1 humanoid.

sections.heading: Tracking deformable terrain modeling and legged robot control
sections.summary: Previous work addressed localized sub-foot deformation using viscoplasticity or granular models, as well as quadruped jump dynamics. However, reinforcement learning for humanoid control on bounded elastic terrains with spatio-temporal coupling remained untouched.
sections.details:
To contextualize this research, previous studies can be grouped into four categories:

### II-A Soft and Deformable Terrain Modeling
Legged locomotion research has traditionally handled soft ground using continuum spring-damper models, granular-media models for sand, or domain randomization of contact parameters. However, these methods focus primarily on localized deflection under the foot. They cannot capture the spatio-temporal dynamics of a bounded elastic membrane where waves propagate away from contact points and vibrations persist long after liftoff.

### II-B Locomotion on Energy-Storing Terrain
Terrains that store energy, like trampolines, act as disturbances but also present opportunities for energy exchange. While quadrupeds have been shown to jump on trampolines while suppressing pitch oscillation, applying this to humanoids—with higher degrees of freedom and greater tipping risk—via learning-based methods remained uncharted.

### II-C Proprioceptive Learning and Sim-to-Real Transfer
Techniques like Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) have shown that history buffers of proprioception can implicitly infer environmental properties, succeeding on humanoids. RIPPLE follows this philosophy, relying entirely on joint and body state history rather than exteroceptive sensors to react to elastic terrain motions.

### II-D Parallel Simulation for Policy Learning
The advent of Isaac Gym, MuJoCo-Warp, and MJLab allows thousands of parallel simulations on a single GPU. RIPPLE builds on this modern stack by integrating pretensioned elastic membranes coupled with deformable contact meshes.

sections.heading: How RIPPLE works: Elastic membrane physics and staged learning
sections.summary: The pretensioned mass-spring lattice ElasticMembrane is integrated into MuJoCo for high-speed GPU-parallel simulation. Training progresses through a curriculum from rigid-ground velocity tracking to jumping, using only the robot's proprioceptive history for action generation.
sections.details:
### III-A Robot–Terrain Dynamics and Simulation Model
Simulating a trampoline membrane without pretension causes excessive sagging under gravity and contact. To address this, the authors designed ElasticMembrane, a square grid of point masses connected by axial and diagonal springs and dampers.

Boundary nodes are fixed in space, while internal nodes (81 nodes with 10 cm spacing for a 1 m × 1 m bed) move in 3D. Setting the rest length of MuJoCo spatial tendons shorter than node distances introduces a pretension $T_0 = 55\,\mathrm{N}$, providing out-of-plane restoring force. A dedicated 2D collision flex mesh shares the node coordinates to compute contact forces with the robot feet accurately. The simulation runs stably at a 2 ms timestep (10 substeps per 50 Hz control step).

### III-B Parallel Simulation and Optimization
Running GPU-parallel simulations with MuJoCo-Warp and MJLab, the authors optimized tendon damping calculations by avoiding sparse matrix writes and omitting unused visualization records, boosting throughput by 21.8%.

### III-C Training Setup and Staged Policy Transfer
The observation space comprises body angular velocity, projected gravity, velocity/height commands, 23-DoF joint positions and velocities, and previous actions across the last 4 timesteps (312 dimensions total). No foot pressure sensors or cameras are used.

Using PPO across 4096 parallel environments on four RTX 5090 GPUs, training follows a staged curriculum:
1. **Flat-VelocityTracking**: Learn basic walking skills on rigid flat ground.
2. **ElasticMembrane-VelocityTracking**: Transfer actor weights and normalizers to the membrane to learn elastic walking and balance.
3. **ElasticMembrane-Jump**: Fine-tune for jumping using commanded height targets, air-time incentives, and liftoff velocity rewards.

Crucially, no task-specific reward shaping is introduced for the elastic terrain; because the environment physics is accurate, adaptive behaviors emerge naturally through reinforcement learning.

### III-D Sim-to-Real Deployment
The trained actor network is exported via ONNX to RKNN and runs onboard the MagicBot Z1 humanoid at 50 Hz, using the exact same proprioceptive interface as in simulation.

A collision-dedicated flex surface (200 triangles), a pretensioned tendon lattice (81 nodes, 420 tendons), and a fixed boundary frame (40 nodes) share node positions to function as one. In the close-up, solid lines indicate axial springs and dashed lines indicate diagonal springs.

sections.heading: Hardware validation and simulation: Riding the trampoline
sections.summary: On a physical MagicBot Z1, the policy succeeded zero-shot in disturbance recovery on a trampoline, turning, entry from rigid ground, and 15 consecutive jumps. Comparative experiments confirm that modeling whole-surface dynamic coupling is essential for sim-to-real transfer.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup and Evaluation Protocol
Hardware experiments used a commercial trampoline (1.5 m diameter, 200 kg capacity). In simulation, standing success was evaluated by letting ground oscillations settle for 20 s, applying random horizontal velocity perturbations (0.1 to 0.9 m/s) at 21 s, 24 s, and 27 s, and checking if the robot maintained orientation and stayed within 0.5 m of the center for 30 s.

### IV-B Zero-Shot Real-World Deployment
On hardware, the ElasticMembrane-VelocityTracking policy exhibited remarkable robustness:
- **Disturbance Rejection**: The robot maintained balance without falling against aggressive disturbances, including arm pulls, kicks to the torso or thighs, and humans stepping on, kicking, or lifting the trampoline frame. Across 657.5 cumulative seconds of deployment, it experienced zero falls.
- **Entry from Rigid Ground**: When stepping from a rigid platform onto the trampoline, the policy absorbed the sudden deflection without hesitation, settling torso oscillations within 2.3 s and 3.3 s into stable walking.
- **Consecutive Jumps**: With ElasticMembrane-Jump, the robot achieved 15 consecutive jumps with >150 ms airtime and ~22 cm foot clearance. Notably, leveraging trampoline elastic energy reduced positive leg work by 39% (from 96 J on flat ground to 59 J) and peak total power by 32% (from 1.94 kW to 1.33 kW).

In contrast, baselines trained on rigid ground or compliant contact models tripped and fell almost immediately upon stepping onto the real trampoline.

### IV-C Impact of Terrain Modeling on Transfer
Comparing four simulation terrain models (CompliantContact, IndependentSprings, BouncyPlate, and ElasticMembrane), CompliantContact-DR failed to transfer to dynamic surfaces (8.0% success on ElasticMembrane). Conversely, policies trained on ElasticMembrane achieved standing success rates of at least 98.7% under 0.3 m/s disturbances across all four terrains. Training on a surface that has mass, elasticity, and dynamic state evolution is clearly critical.

### IV-D Robustness to Stiffness and Bed Size
The policy maintained high success across stiffness scaling from 0.35x to 2.8x, and achieved 100% success on rigid ground (infinite stiffness). It also tolerated bed diameters from 1 m to 7 m, explaining why calibration-free real-world transfer was possible.

### IV-E Additional Application Scenarios
Using the same fixed policy, the robot crossed seven simulated environments—including suspension bridges, bamboo rafts, safety nets, and air domes—maintaining forward walking without falling and with zero retraining.

sections.heading: Why did it work? Insights and remaining hurdles
sections.summary: The boundary-clamped elastic membrane provided an implicit stiffness curriculum that drove high generalization. However, precise physical identification of real trampolines and further simulator throughput gains remain open challenges.
sections.details:
### V-A Physical Insights and Success Factors
Why did the ElasticMembrane-trained policy generalize so broadly? The authors suggest that an 'implicit stiffness curriculum' naturally emerged.

A clamped membrane is softest at the center and becomes progressively stiffer toward the boundaries. As the robot steps in place, tracks velocity commands toward the edge, and transitions off the bed, it experiences a continuous spectrum of stiffness within single episodes. This built-in variation instills robustness across a wide range of stiffnesses without needing explicit domain randomization.

Furthermore, rebound height comparisons (a rigid ball dropped on ElasticMembrane bounced 361 mm, storing and returning far more energy than other models) show that training in the most energetically dynamic environment makes transferring to gentler terrains much easier.

### V-B Limitations and Future Work
The paper notes several limitations:
- The real trampoline lacked precise quantitative system identification for load-deflection and rebound responses, relying on qualitative matching.
- For bed spans exceeding 8 m, gravitational sag exceeded 0.9 m, causing immediate torque saturation and falls upon spawn (bounding the operational envelope).
- GPU throughput in the MuJoCo-Warp calculation pipeline still has room for computational optimization.
- Scenarios like suspension bridges and bamboo rafts have currently only been validated in simulation.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A future where humanoids ride dynamic waves
sections.summary: RIPPLE establishes a sim-to-real framework for humanoid control on large-deformation elastic terrains using only proprioception. With code planned for release, it provides a solid foundation for dynamic legged locomotion.
sections.details:
This study provides the first demonstration of a humanoid robot standing, walking, and jumping stably on elastic terrains where the entire surface dynamically deforms and couples.

By combining GPU-parallel simulation of the pretensioned ElasticMembrane model with a staged curriculum from rigid ground, proprioceptive-only policies transferred zero-shot to a physical trampoline without vision or tactile sensing. The policy exhibited impressive robustness across variations in stiffness and geometry, while uncovering exciting behaviors such as saving leg energy during jumping by exploiting surface rebound.

RIPPLE's simulation environment and training code are slated for open-source release. Breaking free from the assumption of rigid ground, this work represents a major milestone in enabling humanoids to literally 'ride the wave' on soft, dynamic surfaces.

takeaways: Modeling whole-surface spatio-temporal coupling (energy storage and rebound) via mass and pretension—not just localized sub-foot compliance—is the decisive factor for sim-to-real transfer on elastic terrains.
A boundary-clamped membrane acts as an implicit stiffness curriculum ranging from soft (center) to rigid (edges), fostering broad stiffness adaptation without explicit domain randomization.
Using joint encoders and IMU history alone, proprioception is fully sufficient to infer and adapt to the dynamic state of deforming ground without vision or foot force sensors.
Jumping on elastic surfaces naturally prompts energy-saving coordination, reducing positive leg work by ~39% compared to flat ground by utilizing surface recoil.
limitations: Precise system identification of spring constants and damping properties for the physical trampoline was not performed, leaving model matching qualitative.
Hardware limits emerge at very large spans (≥8 m), where gravitational sag causes immediate torque saturation at touchdown.
Compelling deployment scenarios like suspension bridges, bamboo rafts, and air domes remain verified only in simulation, awaiting future real-world hardware tests.
